newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama newspaper undeterred by government moves.
newsitem.headline: Panama newspaper undeterred by government moves.

text.p: Panama's leading newspaper said on Wednesday a government decision not to renew the work permit of one of its senior reporters would not deter it from carrying on with investigative journalism.

The government said on Tuesday that Gustavo Gorriti, a prize-winning Peruvian journalist and associate editor of La Prensa, had until Aug. 28 to leave the country. It argued there were enough Panamanians to fill his post.
La Prensa general manager Juan Luis Correa said the measure "will not diminish our efforts in continuing to do the quality of journalism that La Prensa has always done since its beginning."

Gorriti, 49, who has been living in Panama for a year, told Reuters this week the decision was apparently made because of "the investigations I have published and to prevent more publications in the future."

Gorriti had recently reported on corruption, money laundering and political scandals, including alleged financial contributions from a reputed Colombian drug lord to President Ernesto Perez Balladares' 1994 election campaign.

The U.S. Embassy said on Wednesday that "the government's decision to revoke the residency status of a world-class journalist such as Gustavo Gorriti raises questions about Panama's commitments to freedom of the press." But a spokeswoman said "the embassy did not question the Panamanian government authority to enforce its immigration laws."
The Inter-American Press Association's (IAPA) chairman of press freedom, Danilo Arbilla, said it was "difficult not to see this as reprisals for Gorriti's investigative work."

The Human Rights Watch/Americas organization has criticized the Panamanian government's decision, as has the United States-based Committee To Protect Journalists and the Brussels-based International Federation of Journalists.

Local press, devoting long articles to "the Gorriti case," has accused the government of resorting to strong-arm tactics used by the former military regime of Gen. Manuel Noriega, when journalists were harassed, detained or expelled. The government has categorically denied it was clamping down on press freedom or "persecuting" Gorriti or La Prensa.
